demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Amina, a 47‑year‑old African‑American architect, recalls the night she was driving home from a late‑evening meeting in her sleek office building, when the sudden screech of tires shattered her quiet. She had been distracted by a phone call, and as she eased off the accelerator she saw a woman standing on the crosswalk, unaware of the turning car. In a split second the collision occurred: her car slid into the pedestrian, shattering her front bumper and sending the woman crashing into the pavement. The woman’s scream, the crunch of broken glass, and the smell of oil lingered long after the ambulance had left the scene. The guilt that flooded her was not merely a sense of responsibility; Amina had always seen herself as a careful, meticulous planner. After the crash she began to tell herself, “I should have been more careful,” and “It could have been worse.” This self‑critical rumination made her feel isolated from the people who had once shared her laughter in the lobby of her firm. The more she compared herself to the other architects who seemed to glide through their projects without mishap, the deeper she felt her own identity had frayed, leaving her unrecognizable. The memory of the night has become fragmented whenever she tries to recall it deliberately. She opens her mind to the scene, but her thoughts drift to the blueprints she was working on, the way her hand hovered over the drafting table, and the echo of her own breath. When the memory slips back into her mind, it is not a smooth recollection but a disjointed flash: she tastes the metallic tang of oil and feels the shock of her own heart beating against the chest wall. The sudden taste and the echo of the woman’s cry pull her into the moment, but instead of helping her process it, the experience reinforces the sense that she is different, that she has become a stranger to her own life. The vivid taste triggers her to rehearse mental rituals, silently reciting the steps of a safe driving route she never had before, hoping that if she repeats the ritual she might avoid a repeat of the accident. This mental looping feeds her belief that she is not in control, and each repetition deepens her feeling of isolation. At work, the office hums with the click of keyboards and the distant thud of a construction crane. Amina finds herself standing too close to the glass window, watching the building’s new façade as it shifts in the light, and she hears the phone ring and answers it with a quick “Yes,” only to startle at the sudden ping of the elevator alarm. The false alarms—ordinary sounds that trigger her hypervigilant state—make her feel as if danger is hovering at every corner. She becomes unable to concentrate on the complex structural calculations, her mind always drifting back to the taste of oil, the sound of her own heart, and the image of the wounded woman. When she feels this threat looming, she automatically retreats into her mental rituals, believing that each time she enacts them she can ward off the danger she fears. Yet the rituals never stop the alarms; the pattern of startle and ritual persists, and with each cycle she feels more alienated from her colleagues, who laugh and move on while she stands rooted in fear. Her maladaptive strategies, in turn, pull her memory back into sharp focus. By replaying the scene over and over in her head, she sharpens the taste of oil and the echo of the woman’s cry, reinforcing the vividness of the memory. The memory’s clarity magnifies her sense of isolation, making her feel that she is unrecognizable, as if her own body has been reshaped by the trauma. In this loop, each element feeds the other: the threat she perceives forces her into rituals; the rituals reinforce the threat; the threat distorts her memory; the memory strengthens the rituals. At the end of a long day, she returns home, hears the front door click, and again rehearses her mental safe route, believing that by doing so she can keep her fear at bay. Amina has finally reached out for help because the endless cycle has begun to erode her relationships. She notices her husband growing frustrated at her avoidance of evening conversations, her projects slipping behind schedule, and her own anxiety becoming a constant companion. She fears that if she does not break this loop, she will become permanently trapped in a state where she feels alone and unrecognizable, a stranger to the architect she once was. She hopes to regain control over her thoughts, to quiet the false alarms, and to find a way to let the memory of the night fade into the background rather than dominate her present life.
